findings.mechanism: size_orders converts notional into share counts by dividing by panel["close"], so the execution price assumed is the raw closing print with no half-spread, no offset and no size-dependent impact. The only charge in the module is a flat COST_BPS = 2.0 on weight.diff().abs(), a commission-scale number with no spread component. That is inconsistent with the strategy this file describes: the target is an open-to-close move, so every unit of weight is crossed twice per day. weight.diff().abs() charges nothing for a position held at constant weight, even though such a position is fully liquidated and re-established each session.
findings.title: Orders priced at the unadjusted closing print for a strategy whose label is a daily open-to-close round trip

findings.mechanism: size_orders computes notional = weight * capital and returns notional / close as the share count. capital is a free float parameter with no ceiling, and the resulting share count is never compared against any measure of the name's liquidity. No volume, dollar-volume or ADV column is referenced anywhere in this module, so the panel has no field that could support a participation cap even if one were wanted. Doubling capital doubles every position with no change in the reported net return - the backtest's PnL is scale-invariant, which is only true if every name can absorb an arbitrary order at the close.
findings.title: Share counts scale linearly with an unbounded capital argument and are never checked against traded volume

findings.mechanism: add_label defines the target as intraday_move_t = close_t/open_t - 1. add_features puts two same-bar features next to it: overnight_gap_t = open_t/close_{t-1} - 1 and close_to_close_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1. Their ratio is the label exactly: (1 + close_to_close_t) / (1 + overnight_gap_t) = close_t/open_t = 1 + intraday_move_t. The target is not literally in X, but it is a closed-form function of two columns that are, and a model recovers it to machine precision. Every fold score measures this identity rather than any forecast.
findings.title: Target is algebraically recoverable from close_to_close and overnight_gap

findings.mechanism: The label for bar t is built from open_t and close_t. realised_vol at row t is a 60-bar trailing std whose final term depends on close_t: the window closes on the same bar the label describes, with no gap. The trailing rolling() call is what makes this look safe to a pattern matcher, but 'trailing' here means trailing up to and including the labelled bar, not up to the last observable bar. Large-magnitude label days carry a mechanically inflated realised_vol. Aligning it honestly requires a shift(1), since at the decision point - the open of bar t - close_t does not yet exist.
findings.title: realised_vol window terminates on the same bar the label is drawn from

findings.mechanism: load_fundamentals documents two dates on each quarterly record: period_end, the last day of the quarter the numbers describe, and filing_date, the day the report was actually released, 'typically six to nine weeks later'. The merge keys the daily panel's date to period_end, i.e. to the effective date rather than the availability date. So net_income and market_cap for a quarter ending 31-Mar land on the 31-Mar bar, six to nine weeks before the filing that first published them; earnings_yield is derived from the same premature values, and the groupby-ffill then carries that unpublished number forward across every day of the lag window. A trader standing at the 31-Mar close could not have known these numbers. The correct key is filing_date (or a merge_asof backward on filing_date), not period_end.
findings.title: Quarterly fundamentals joined on period_end instead of filing_date

findings.mechanism: add_label defines the target as intraday_move = close[t] / open[t] - 1, whose decision point is the open of bar t. close_to_close at row t embeds close[t] - the exact price that terminates the label - into a feature attached to that same row. Anyone positioning at open[t] cannot observe close[t]; the feature is only resolvable once the labelled move has already happened. net_return pays the strategy that same close_to_close series, so the backtest compounds returns generated by a feature unavailable at live decision time.
findings.title: close_to_close feature contains the same bar's close, which is the label's terminal price

findings.mechanism: The window is trailing, so a pattern matcher sees nothing wrong, but the last observation entering rolling(60).std() at row t depends on close[t]. Since the label is the same session's open-to-close move, the decision timestamp for row t is open[t], and close[t] is still unknown then. realised_vol at t is partly a function of the very move being predicted - contaminated in the same direction as the label, diluted by 1/60 but systematically. It needs a shift(1) to be computable at the open of bar t.
findings.title: Trailing volatility window includes the current bar's own return

findings.mechanism: The docstring states reference is one row per ticker carrying sector, country and listing venue - there is no as-of column, and the merge keys on ticker alone. The classification as it stands on the day the reference file was pulled is broadcast onto every historical bar. GICS reclassifications, country-of-domicile changes and venue migrations all get retro-applied: a name reclassified into Technology in 2021 appears as Technology back in 2015, a fact no one holding it in 2015 could have known.
findings.title: Sector reference table has no effective date, so today's classification is applied to all history

findings.mechanism: attach_sector merges reference onto the time-indexed panel on ticker alone, and the docstring states reference is one row per ticker carrying sector, country and listing venue. There is no date, from_date/to_date or as_of column in the join key, so whatever value each ticker holds today is broadcast backwards over every historical row. None of the three attributes is time-invariant: sectors get reclassified, country of domicile changes with redomiciliations, and listing venue changes with transfers and uplistings. The bias runs the same way for membership: a table assembled today contains only tickers that still exist, so any name acquired or delisted mid-sample either joins to nothing or joins to a symbol since reassigned to a different company.
findings.title: Present-day per-ticker reference table joined onto the whole historical panel

findings.mechanism: split() builds a GroupKFold over the daily equity panel and passes groups=panel["ticker"], so the only guarantee is that a given name is never in both folds. The date axis is not used at all: every fold's training rows cover the same full date range as the test rows, including the exact sessions being predicted. For any test row on date D for ticker A, the training set contains rows for tickers B, C, ... on that same date D with their realised same-session moves as labels. Equity returns on a common date share market and sector factor exposure - sector is even joined on in attach_sector - so the model can learn date D's realised factor return from the training names and apply it to the held-out name on date D. The docstring shows the grouping was intended as the whole of the safety argument.
findings.title: GroupKFold grouped by ticker leaves train and test folds fully overlapping in calendar time

findings.mechanism: ROUNDS records the configuration changes that produced the headline number, and report's docstring states the writeup uses round 5. Round 5's change is dropping the two sectors that turned out worst. 'Worst-performing' is a ranking over realised returns across the study period, including the holdout that begins at HOLDOUT_START and is the very window report scores on. Nothing computes that ranking from data ending before the holdout, so the names remaining are exactly those whose sectors are already known to have done well. The Sharpe jump from 0.71 to 0.94 is the size of that selection effect, not an improvement in the model.
findings.title: Round 5 universe excludes the two worst-performing sectors, a whole-sample outcome

findings.mechanism: ROUNDS records five successive model revisions, each scored on the period returned by holdout(), which is always the same fixed slice. The Sharpe column climbs monotonically 0.31 to 0.94 precisely because each change was kept or discarded on the basis of the previous round's holdout number: round 3 dropped what round 2 added, round 4 widened a window, and round 5 excluded the two worst-performing sectors - worst-performing on the holdout itself, a parameter fitted directly to the evaluation data. report() then returns that fifth configuration's holdout Sharpe as the headline. There is no sweep object and no explicit grid, so nothing mechanical fires, but the researcher has performed a five-trial search with the holdout as the objective, and no untouched period remains.
findings.quoted_line: """Headline number for the writeup: round 5, evaluated on the holdout."""
findings.title: Headline Sharpe is the fifth revision scored on the same holdout used to choose all five
